title: Commits are snapshots; amend only what is private
explanation:
`git commit` records the snapshot you set up in the index — anything you didn't stage stays modified in your working directory for a later commit. Give the message inline with `-m "..."`, written as a short imperative summary ("Add cafe menu"). Each commit stores a pointer to its parent, so the commits form a history.

If you notice right away that you forgot a file or mistyped the message, `git commit --amend` redoes the **last** commit: it takes the current index (plus a new message with `-m`, or the old one with `--no-edit`) and builds a new commit that *replaces* the old one. It is as if the old commit never happened.

```bash
git commit -m "Add cafe menu"
git add forgotten.md
git commit --amend --no-edit     # same message, now including forgotten.md
```

That replacement is exactly why amending is only for **local** commits. If you already pushed the commit, others may have built on it; amending and force-pushing rewrites history under them. For published work, make a new commit instead.
keyIdeas: A commit records the staged snapshot, not your whole working directory.
`-m` sets the message inline; keep it a short imperative summary.
`--amend` replaces the last commit with a new one built from the index.
Amend only commits that are still local; fix published work with a new commit.

workedExample.problem: You commit `menu.md` with the message `Add menu`, then realise you forgot `prices.md` and want the message to say `Add menu and prices`. The commit is unpushed. Fix it so history shows one commit, not two.
steps: Stage the forgotten file: `git add prices.md`.
Amend with a new message: `git commit --amend -m "Add menu and prices"` — this rebuilds the last commit from the index.
Confirm the count did not grow and the new commit contains both files.

Run it in a throwaway folder:
```sh
git init -q -b trunk shop && cd shop
printf '# Shop\n' > README.md && git add README.md && git commit -q -m 'Initial commit'
printf 'tea\n' > menu.md; printf 'tea 3\n' > prices.md
git add menu.md && git commit -q -m 'Add menu'
before=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
git add prices.md
git commit -q --amend -m 'Add menu and prices'
[ "$(git rev-list --count HEAD)" = 2 ]                 # still two commits
[ "$(git log -1 --format=%s)" = 'Add menu and prices' ]
[ "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" != "$before" ]              # a new commit replaced the old one
git ls-tree --name-only HEAD | grep -qx prices.md
echo ok
```
workedExample.answer: Two commits in total (the initial one and the amended `Add menu and prices`), and the amended commit has a new id because it replaced the old one.

pitfalls: Amending a commit that is already pushed, forcing teammates to reconcile rewritten history.
Expecting unstaged edits to be included in a commit or an amend — only the index is used.
Writing vague messages like "fix" or "stuff" that make `git log` useless later.

citations.quote: Remember that the commit records the snapshot you set up in your staging area. Anything you didn't stage is still sitting there modified
you can type your commit message inline with the commit command by specifying it after a -m flag
the next commit stores a pointer to the commit that came immediately before it.
This command takes your staging area and uses it for the commit.
Effectively, it's as if the previous commit never happened, and it won't show up in your repository history.
Only amend commits that are still local and have not been pushed somewhere. Amending previously pushed commits and force pushing the branch will cause problems for your collaborators.
